fixtures.name: am_profile_hang
fixtures.command: adb shell am profile start --sampling 1000 com.example.composefixture /data/local/tmp/aes_hang.trace; adb shell am broadcast -f 0x10000000 -n com.example.composefixture/.AnrReceiver -a com.example.composefixture.PROVOKE_ANR; wait until 45s after the broadcast; adb shell am profile stop com.example.composefixture; adb exec-out cat /data/local/tmp/aes_hang.trace
fixtures.description: An ART method trace of the fixture app, sampled every 1000 us by `am profile start --sampling` while AnrReceiver held its main thread in Thread.sleep for 40 s -- a hung app, seen from inside without root on a `user` build. The ground truth the v0.9.0 hang sampler is parsed against (vault: 'Sampling a Hung App Without Root'). BINARY, written byte for byte: a text header (`*version` / `3` / key=value lines including `clock=dual` / `*threads` / `*methods` / `*end`), then a little-endian body starting with the magic `SLOW`. What a parser written from memory gets wrong: the records are TRANSITIONS, not samples -- a 40 s block is one enter and one exit 40 s apart, not 40,000 rows; the stack the thread already had when profiling began is replayed as enters at the first sample; and under clock=dual each record carries the thread-CPU clock BEFORE the wall clock, so across the sleep the CPU clock moves by milliseconds and only the wall clock shows the hang. Thread.sleep appears three times nested (three overloads), so 'the frame under the sleep' is the first frame that is not a Thread.sleep. Taken 10 s after launch, so that Jetpack ProfileInstaller's one-shot worker thread has come and gone first: in 1 of 3 recorder runs on 2026-10-16 the app aborted (ART thread.cc:2698 CHECK) as that worker exited under the sampler (see TRACE_QUIET_BEFORE_S). Note too that `am broadcast` did not return until the receiver timed out (broadcast_returned_after_s).

fixtures.description: `am profile start` to a path on shared storage. Refused: exit **255**, stdout empty, and on stderr an SELinux denial (`avc:  denied  { write } ... scontext=u:r:system_server:s0 tcontext=u:object_r:fuse:s0`) RUN TOGETHER with the next sentence on the same line, no newline between them, then 'Error: Unable to open file: <path>' and 'Consider using a file under /data/local/tmp/'. It is system_server that opens the file, not the app and not the shell, which is why /sdcard -- writable from `adb shell` -- is still refused. The refusal LEAVES A 0-BYTE FILE behind (see left_behind in this entry), so a caller that takes 'the trace file exists' as proof profiling started is fooled; the exit status is the only reliable signal.

fixtures.name: am_start_wait_settings
fixtures.description: A successful `am start -W`, cold. Two traps for a parser written from memory. fixtures.description:
The permission state of an installed package, which is what `privacy_manager --list` parses and what proves a grant took effect. There is NO 'granted permissions:' section -- the header privacy_manager looked for, which is why --list always answered with two empty lists. The real headers, at four spaces of indent under `Package [<pkg>]`, are 'declared permissions:' (name: prot=...), 'requested permissions:' (bare names), 'install permissions:' (name: granted=<bool>), and -- nested one level deeper, under 'User 0:' -- 'runtime permissions:' (name: granted=<bool>, flags=[...]).
Deskclock is recorded rather than the fixture app because it is an UPDATED system app, so the dump repeats all four sections a second time under the top-level 'Hidden system packages:' header. Measured: that copy is NOT stale -- granting READ_CALENDAR flips `granted` in both copies -- so the cost of reading it is a doubled list rather than a wrong value, and taking the first occurrence of each section is what keeps it out. It also carries both outcomes: POST_NOTIFICATIONS granted=true, READ_CALENDAR and READ_MEDIA_AUDIO granted=false.
